A sparse autoencoder gives you a dictionary of directions in activation space
and a claim that those directions are more interpretable than neurons. That
claim is doing a lot of work, and this note is about where it stops holding.

## The setup

Given activations $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, an SAE learns an encoder and decoder
such that

$$
\hat{x} = W_{\text{dec}} f(x) + b, \qquad f(x) = \text{ReLU}(W_{\text{enc}}(x - b)),
$$

trained to minimise reconstruction error under an $\ell_1$ penalty on $f(x)$:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\lVert x - \hat{x} \rVert_2^2}_{\text{reconstruction}} + \lambda \underbrace{\lVert f(x) \rVert_1}_{\text{sparsity}}.
$$

The interpretability claim is that the columns of $W_{\text{dec}}$ correspond
to human-legible features [@cunningham2023sparse]. The mechanistic claim —
which is different, and stronger — is that those features are the units the
model itself computes over [@olah2020zoom].

## Where the two claims come apart

::: {.callout-note}
## The short version
A dictionary element can be legible to you and still not be a variable the
model uses. Legibility is a property of the projection; causal relevance has
to be tested separately.
:::

Three things to check before treating a feature as mechanistic:

1. **Ablation actually changes behaviour.** If zeroing the feature leaves the
   downstream logits untouched, you have found a correlate, not a cause.
2. **The effect survives a better baseline.** Mean ablation and zero ablation
   disagree, sometimes badly — I wrote about this
   [separately](../../insights/2026-08-02-one-gpu-setup/).
3. **The feature is stable across seeds.** Dictionaries trained on the same
   activations with different seeds should recover overlapping features. Often
   they don't.

## A quick illustration

```{python}
#| label: fig-sparsity
#| fig-cap: "Reconstruction error against dictionary sparsity. The elbow is where legibility and fidelity start trading off."
#| eval: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

l0 = np.array([4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128])
mse = np.array([0.42, 0.27, 0.16, 0.11, 0.09, 0.085])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.2))
ax.plot(l0, mse, marker="o", color="#11707E")
ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
ax.set_xlabel("mean $L_0$ (active features per token)")
ax.set_ylabel("reconstruction MSE")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
```

## What I'd want to see next

An SAE paper that reports, for its headline features, the ablation effect size
alongside the interpretability score. Right now those two numbers rarely
appear in the same table.
